hints: Think of two very different functional groups that can both be converted into a secondary amine, one by forming a new C-N bond and one by reducing a C=O to CH2.
For the C-N bond forming route, recall what type of reagent attacks a halogenoalkane and what small molecule is needed to supply the second ethyl group.
For the reduction route, recall which amide would give $(C_2H_5)_2NH$ on reduction and which powerful reducing agent reduces amides but not alkenes.
Remember the conditions that favour nucleophilic substitution in halogenoalkanes, heating in an alcoholic solvent in a sealed apparatus.
walkthrough:
See diethylamine as a secondary amine to build**
You have $(C_2H_5)_2NH$. That is a secondary amine with two ethyl groups on nitrogen. You can build it by attaching an ethyl group to ethylamine, or you can start with the nitrogen already attached to two carbons but with a carbonyl to reduce.

Route by nucleophilic substitution**
Picture $CH_3CH_2Cl$ with the polar $C^{\delta+}-Cl^{\delta-}$ bond. Ethylamine, $CH_3CH_2NH_2$, has a lone pair on N and acts as a nucleophile. It attacks the $\delta+$ carbon, displaces $Cl^-$ and forms $(C_2H_5)_2NH$. This needs heat in ethanol under pressure in a sealed tube to keep volatile reactants in contact.

Route by reduction of an amide**
Now think backwards from the amide. To get two ethyl groups after reduction, you need $CH_3CONHC_2H_5$, N-ethyl ethanamide. Reduction converts $C=O$ to $CH_2$, so $CH_3-C(=O)-NH-C_2H_5$ becomes $CH_3-CH_2-NH-C_2H_5$.

Choose the correct reducing agent**
Amides are very stable to mild reduction. Only the powerful hydride donor $LiAlH_4$, in dry ether followed by aqueous work up, will reduce an amide to an amine. Do not use $NaBH_4$ or $H_2/Ni$ here, they do not reduce amides.

Final answer: Reaction one: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ + $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ heated under pressure in ethanol to give $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}$.
Reaction two: $\text{CH}_3\text{CONHC}_2\text{H}_5$ (N-ethyl ethanamide) reduced by $\text{LiAlH}_4$ to give $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}$.

hints: Recall that basicity in water means ability of the nitrogen lone pair to accept $H^+$ to form an alkylammonium ion.
Compare the environment of the nitrogen lone pair in $NH_3$, in $(C_2H_5)_2NH$ with alkyl groups, and in $C_6H_5NH_2$ attached to a benzene ring.
Think how delocalisation into the ring versus electron donation from ethyl groups changes electron density on nitrogen.
walkthrough:
Link basicity to the lone pair**
A base accepts $H^+$, for example $R_2NH + H^+ \rightarrow R_2NH_2^+$. The easier the lone pair on nitrogen is to donate, the stronger the base. So compare how available that lone pair is in the three compounds.

Why phenylamine is weakest**
In $C_6H_5NH_2$ the p orbital on N overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring. The lone pair is delocalised into the ring. That lowers electron density on N, so it is much less ready to bond to $H^+$. The resulting phenylammonium ion is also less stabilised.

Why diethylamine is strongest**
In $(C_2H_5)_2NH$ each ethyl group pushes electron density toward N by the positive inductive effect. That increases electron density on N, makes the lone pair more available, and helps stabilise the positive charge on the conjugate acid $(C_2H_5)_2NH_2^+$. Ammonia, $NH_3$, has no ring delocalisation and no alkyl donation, so it sits in the middle.

Final answer: least basic phenylamine < ammonia < diethylamine most basic.
Basicity depends on availability of lone pair on N to accept $H^+$.
In phenylamine the lone pair is delocalised into / overlaps with the benzene pi system, less available.
In diethylamine ethyl groups are electron donating, increasing electron density on N, more available.

hints: Recall the two step sequence at $4^{\circ}C$: phenylamine with $HNO_2$ gives a diazonium ion P, then P couples with phenol in alkali.
Think what linkage joins the two aromatic rings in the final coloured product and where it is commonly used.
walkthrough:
Track P then Q**
At $4^{\circ}C$, $C_6H_5NH_2 + HNO_2 + HCl$ gives the diazonium salt P, $C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-$. This $N_2^+$ group is a strong electrophile. Under alkaline conditions phenol exists as phenoxide, which is highly activated for electrophilic substitution.

Draw the coupling product**
Coupling occurs para to the $OH$ group to give $C_6H_5-N=N-C_6H_4-OH$. That $N=N$ bridge between two benzene rings is the azo group, so circle $N=N$. The extended conjugated system absorbs visible light, giving an intense orange colour. Such azo compounds are widely used as dyes.

Final answer: Compound Q is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N=N C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH}$, 4-hydroxyazobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-N=N-C_6H_4-OH$ (para isomer), with the $N=N$ azo group circled.
Use: dye / colouring agent for fabrics, inks or indicators.

hints: Start by labelling the polar $C=O$ bond in $CH_3COCl$ and locating the nucleophilic lone pair on the secondary amine.
Recall the charge pattern in the tetrahedral intermediate after N attacks the carbonyl carbon.
Think which two sigma bonds must break to restore $C=O$ and release the leaving group plus a proton.
Balance atoms to find the small second product formed alongside $CH_3CON(C_2H_5)_2$.
walkthrough:
Set up box one with dipoles and lone pairs**
Look at $H_3C-C(Cl)=O$. Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so mark $C^{\delta+}$ and $O^{\delta-}$. Show all lone pairs: two lone pairs on the carbonyl O, three on Cl, one on the amine N. The amine N is the nucleophile. Draw a curly arrow starting at the N lone pair and pointing to the $C^{\delta+}$ of the carbonyl.

Form the tetrahedral intermediate in box two**
When the N-C bond forms, the $C=O$ pi bond breaks onto O. You get $H_3C-C(Cl)(O^-)-N^+(H)(C_2H_5)_2$. Carbon is now tetrahedral. Nitrogen has four bonds so it carries a + charge, oxygen has three lone pairs and a single bond so it carries a - charge. Show those charges clearly.

Collapse the intermediate with three arrows**
To reform the stable $C=O$, draw a curly arrow from an $O^-$ lone pair back to form $C=O$. That pushes out the leaving group: draw a curly arrow from the $C-Cl$ bond onto Cl to give $Cl^-$. At the same time the $N^+-H$ proton is lost: draw a curly arrow from the $N-H$ bond back onto N to neutralise the + charge. In practice a second amine or $Cl^-$ picks up the $H^+$.

Identify both products in box three**
Reforming $C=O$ gives the amide $H_3C-C(=O)-N(C_2H_5)_2$, N,N-diethylethanamide. The $H^+$ from nitrogen and $Cl^-$ from the acyl chloride combine to give the second product, $HCl$. That balances $CH_3COCl + HN(C_2H_5)_2 \rightarrow CH_3CON(C_2H_5)_2 + HCl$.

Final answer: Box one: $\text{C}=\text{O}$ shown as $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$, lone pairs on O, Cl and N shown, curly arrow from N lone pair to $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$.
Box two: tetrahedral intermediate $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}(\text{Cl})(\text{O}^-)-\text{N}^+(\text{H})(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2$ with correct + on N and - on O.
Curly arrows: N-H bond to N, C-Cl bond to Cl, $\text{O}^-$ lone pair to reform $\text{C}=\text{O}$.
Box three second product: $\text{HCl}$.

hints: Recall the two stage name for nucleophilic attack on an acyl chloride to form a tetrahedral intermediate followed by loss of chloride.
walkthrough:
Name the two stages**
First the nucleophile adds to the $C=O$ to give a tetrahedral intermediate, then the intermediate eliminates $Cl^-$ as $C=O$ reforms. That two word description is addition-elimination.
